title: Half a Team at Xerox
text:
In the early 1990s, Ruth Wageman studied customer service technicians at Xerox, the people who traveled to clients to repair copiers. Xerox was reorganizing them into teams, and the teams differed in how their work and their rewards were set up.

Some teams were designed so that technicians truly shared the work and were rewarded on team results. Others worked mostly as individuals with individual rewards. Many were hybrids, with some shared tasks, some individual ones, and a mix of team and individual rewards. Wageman, then at Harvard, studied about 150 of these teams, measuring how they operated and how well they performed on Xerox's service measures.

The clearly designed teams did well, whether they were fully interdependent or largely individual. The hybrid teams did worst. Members of mixed teams carried the costs of teamwork, such as coordination and meetings, without getting its benefits, and their groups showed poorer working processes and lower member satisfaction. The lesson Wageman drew was that half measures are risky: the way the work is organized and the way people are rewarded should point in the same direction.
lesson: Decide whether a group is really a team or a set of individuals, and design the work and the rewards to match. Halfway arrangements tend to get the worst of both.
source: Wageman, R. (1995). Interdependence and group effectiveness. Administrative Science Quarterly, 40(1), 145-180.
